basis: The forceful lateral takeoff and controlled landing train lateral power, planned repositioning, and dynamic postural control.

name: Step-Ups
basis: Repeated steps or knee raises recruit substantial lower-body muscle mass at a moderate pace. They can develop basic aerobic/local endurance and simple interlimb timing, without high-force or maximal-speed claims.

name: Lateral Step-Ups

name: Calf Raises on a Step
basis: The step permits loaded calf work over a larger ankle range. The direct stimulus remains local strength/endurance, with a modest active-range contribution.

name: Decline Push-Ups
basis: The asymmetric, inclined, or low traveling pushing lever increases local force demand beyond a standard push-up. The fixed demonstrated variation supports substantial task-specific strength and endurance.

name: Bench Hip Thrusts
basis: The demanding knee/hip lever or unilateral support directly loads the posterior chain/adductors. It supplies substantial local strength and endurance without implying a universal strength level.

name: Elevated Forearm Pike Scapular Push-Ups

name: Sideways Bear Crawl
basis: Traveling on multiple supports recruits substantial muscle mass while practicing predictable contralateral foot/hand placement. This supports moderate aerobic and local endurance plus task-specific coordination.

name: Bunny Hops
basis: Repeated short elastic hops load the ankle plantar flexors and practice basic takeoff/landing rhythm. The small displacement limits the high-force power claim.

name: Burpee Broad Jumps
basis: Full-body transitions followed by deliberate horizontal takeoffs combine vigorous whole-body/local endurance with substantial repeated lower-body power and sequencing.

name: Log Rolls
basis: The roll, sit-through, or changing-support transition practices linked trunk/limb timing and some local endurance. Floor contact supplies a stable support context.

name: Seated Buttock Walks
basis: Controlled unresisted joint movement practices basic available range. Activation, ordinary bracing, and merely moving a limb are not treated as substantial strength or endurance training.
